newsitem.title: JAPAN: Bankers Trust unlikely to take over NCB - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bankers Trust unlikely to take over NCB - analysts.

text.p: The alliance between Bankers Trust and Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB) is unlikely to lead to a fully fledged takeover of NCB by the U.S. investment bank, analysts and financial sources said on Thursday.
If Bankers Trust takes a stake in NCB, it would be the first time a foreign bank has owned part of a Japanese bank.

But the analysts said the alliance was unlikely to go beyond a limited business partnership as the troubled Japanese long-term credit bank was not a very attractive takeover target in terms of return on equity.
"The agreement announced this morning would probably be a simple business alliance," said Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
"It will make it easier for NCB to implement its restructuring programme, but its ROE (return on equity) is too low for the U.S. bank to consider any takeover move," he said.

NCB and Bankers Trust New York Corp said earlier on Thursday that they had agreed on a business tie-up under which the U.S. bank would securitise some of NCB's loans, boosting liquidity, and help maintain services to NCB customers after the bank's planned withdrawal from overseas operations. The two partners said they would also consider a capital tie-up. The agreement will be signed in late April.
Hideichiro Nishimura, an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics Inc, agreed that a takeover was unlikely.
"It is unthinkable that Bankers Trust would take over NCB," he said.
The mutual equity participation is likely to be a limited cross-shareholding between the two banks, he said.
On April 1, NCB announced a radical restructuring programme, including withdrawal from overseas operations.

The bank, which is saddled with extensive problem loans, said that it would close five overseas branches -- New York, London, Singapore, Hong Kong and Grand Cayman -- and seven representative offices and also sell its subsidiaries.
However, at that time NCB did not reveal details of its withdrawal strategy and said it would take considerable time to complete the pullout.

Financial sources said that Bankers Trust would not be interested in NCB's overseas banking business. Another U.S. or European bank may acquire NCB's New York branch as Japanese banks have already established a foothold there, they said.
Analysts said that while the tie-up accord would he positive for NCB's restructuring efforts, the bank had work to do to get in shape for Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms.
"To ensure a bright future, NCB must first successfully increase its capital," said Nishimura at Yamaichi Research.
Earlier this week, NCB said that it intends to increase its capital by 290.7 billion yen by issuing ordinary and preferred shares. However, the bank did not announce an issuing schedule.
Despite the restructuring programme, yields on NCB's debentures remain much higher than those on debentures by other long-term credit banks, due to worries about NCB's future, analysts said.
As one of Japan's three long-term credit banks, NCB mainly raises money through issuing debentures instead of taking deposits.

Moody's Investors Service said last week that it would monitor NCB's restructuring to decide the direction of the bank's rating. The rating agency cut NCB's senior debt -- worth some 10 trillion yen -- to junk-bond levels last month.

"Moody's is particularly concerned about the ability of NCB to obtain funding at a price comparable to that of other domestic debenture-issuing banks," Moody's said last week. -- Fumiko Fujisaki, Tokyo Equities
